overview.title: BERT, masked language modeling, RoBERTa
overview.main_topic: How BERT was pretrained (a bidirectional Transformer encoder trained with masked language modeling on unlabeled text), why that produced contextual word representations, and the introduction of RoBERTa and of the three things needed to reuse a pretrained model.
overview.central_idea: BERT is the encoder half of a Transformer, pretrained by hiding about 15% of tokens and predicting them from both sides. The objective needs no labels, so it scales to huge text corpora and yields context-dependent token representations that can be fine-tuned for many tasks. RoBERTa applies the same idea with ten times more data.
overview.importance: Masked language modeling is the self-supervised objective behind the encoder model fine-tuned on IMDb later in this section. Contrasting $p(\text{token}\mid\text{past})$ with $p(\text{token}\mid\text{surrounding})$ separates encoder models (BERT/RoBERTa) from decoder models (GPT, chapter 16).
learning_objectives: Describe BERT's architecture and what 'bidirectional' means for its attention.
Explain masked language modeling and contrast it with causal language modeling.
Explain why MLM pretraining is unsupervised (self-supervised) and why that enables scale.
Distinguish static pretrained word embeddings (chapter 14) from contextual embeddings from a pretrained Transformer.
State how RoBERTa differs from BERT, mainly by its 10x larger pretraining corpus.
List the first requirement for reusing a pretrained model: a matching tokenizer.

summary:
**BERT** was released a year after "Attention Is All You Need." Its structure is exactly the **encoder** of the translation Transformer built in this chapter. It is **bidirectional**: every position attends to positions both before and after it. That makes it good at computing rich representations of input text, but it is not a model for generating text in a loop.

BERT came in sizes from about 100M to 300M parameters, far more than the roughly 14M-parameter translation Transformer, so it needed a lot of training data. The authors therefore used **masked language modeling (MLM)**: replace about 15% of the tokens in a text with a special `[MASK]` token and train the model to recover the originals. A classic (**causal**) language model predicts `p(token|past tokens)`; a masked LM predicts `p(token|surrounding tokens)`. The setup is **unsupervised**: any text can be masked automatically, with no labels, so the authors could use a lot of text, mostly from Wikipedia.

Pretrained word embeddings (chapter 14) were already common, but they give each word a single vector. A pretrained Transformer instead computes a word's representation **in the context** of the surrounding words, at a scale and quality new at the time. Fine-tuned, BERT achieved state-of-the-art results on several NLP benchmarks, starting the shift toward very large pretrained models adapted with only a small amount of fine-tuning.

**Section 15.4.2** uses **RoBERTa** (Robustly Optimized BERT, Liu et al. 2019) instead. It slightly simplifies BERT's architecture, but its main change is more data: **160 GB** of web text vs. BERT's **16 GB**, mainly Wikipedia. Training cost an estimated few hundred thousand dollars, and the model performs noticeably better at an equal parameter count. To use a pretrained model you need several things. The first, a **matching tokenizer**, is introduced at the bottom of the page: text must be tokenized exactly as during pretraining (continued on p.480, which also lists the matching architecture and the pretrained weights).

paragraphs.excerpt: model were released a year after “Attention Is All You Need.” The model structure
paragraphs.what_it_says: BERT's paper and model appeared a year after the Transformer paper (2018). Its structure is exactly the encoder part of the translation Transformer built in this chapter. It is bidirectional: each position can attend to positions before and after it. That makes it good for rich text representations, but not for generating text in a loop.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The `TransformerEncoder` of p.468 uses self-attention with only a padding mask, no causal mask, so information flows in both directions. A generator must predict the next token from the past only. BERT never learned that, since during pretraining it always saw both sides, and nothing in it is designed for autoregressive use.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This splits Transformer models into families: encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) for understanding and classification, decoder-only (GPT, chapter 16) for generation, and encoder-decoder (the translator of section 15.3) for sequence-to-sequence tasks.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Bidirectional attention: for every query position $i$, the attention weights range over all non-padding positions $j$, with $j < i$ and $j > i$ both allowed.

terminology.meaning: Attending to both left and right context of a position (no causal mask).
A Transformer consisting only of encoder blocks; it outputs one contextual vector per input token.

connections: p.470: the decoder's causal attention, which BERT lacks
p.489: summary: encoder uses bidirectional attention, decoder uses causal attention

paragraphs.excerpt: BERT was trained in sizes between 100 million and 300 million parameters, much bigger
paragraphs.what_it_says: BERT was trained at 100M-300M parameters, far larger than the 14M-parameter Transformer of this chapter, so it needed a lot of data. Masked language modeling made that possible: about 15% of tokens are replaced with `[MASK]` and the model predicts the originals. A causal LM predicts p(token | past tokens); a masked LM predicts p(token | surrounding tokens). This is unsupervised, so data is plentiful (mostly Wikipedia). Pretrained word embeddings already existed (chapter 14), but pretraining a whole Transformer gives contextual embeddings, at a new scale and quality. Fine-tuned, BERT set state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, shifting the field toward large pretrained models with light fine-tuning.
paragraphs.what_it_means:
Several ideas are packed together.

1. **Model size drives data needs.** More parameters need more examples to fit without overfitting.
2. **MLM is a fill-in-the-blank game.** The text supplies its own labels, which makes it self-supervised.
3. **Conditioning differs.** A causal LM conditions on one side; an MLM on both. Two-sided context gives better representations but no straightforward way to generate text.
4. **Contextual vs. static embeddings.** A chapter 14 embedding gives "bank" one vector. A pretrained encoder gives "bank" in "river bank" and in "bank account" different vectors, because attention mixes in the context.
5. **Transfer.** Pretrain once on generic text, then fine-tune on specific benchmarks.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual basis of section 15.4. The RoBERTa backbone fine-tuned on IMDb (pp.484-485) was trained with this objective, which is why its token vectors already encode meaning before seeing any review label.
paragraphs.technical_idea: MLM loss: $\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{i \in M} \log p_\theta(x_i \mid \tilde{x})$, where $M$ is the set of masked positions and $\tilde{x}$ is the corrupted sequence. Only masked positions contribute. Beyond the book: BERT actually replaced a chosen token with `[MASK]` 80% of the time, a random token 10%, and left it unchanged 10%, to reduce the mismatch with fine-tuning, where `[MASK]` never appears.

terminology.meaning: Pretraining objective: corrupt a random ~15% of tokens and predict the originals from the remaining context.
A model of $p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$: predicts each token from the preceding ones (section 15.1).
Training targets are derived automatically from the input data; no human annotation is needed.
A token vector that depends on the surrounding words, as produced by a Transformer encoder.
Special vocabulary token that marks a hidden position during MLM pretraining.

paragraphs.excerpt: Instead of using BERT here, let’s use a follow-up model called RoBERTa, short for
paragraphs.what_it_says: The book uses RoBERTa (Robustly Optimized BERT, Liu et al. 2019) instead of BERT. It slightly simplifies BERT's architecture but mainly uses more data: 160 GB of web text vs. BERT's 16 GB mostly from Wikipedia. Training cost an estimated few hundred thousand dollars. With more data, it performs noticeably better at the same parameter count.
paragraphs.what_it_means: RoBERTa shows that BERT was **undertrained**: the same kind of model gets much better with 10x more data and longer training. Beyond the book, RoBERTa's other changes were dropping BERT's next-sentence-prediction objective, re-sampling masks dynamically each epoch instead of fixing them once, larger batches, and a byte-level BPE tokenizer with a ~50K vocabulary (p.480).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It reinforces the lesson of p.478: for Transformers, data scale matters as much as architecture. It also explains the choice: for the same compute at fine-tuning time, RoBERTa gives better accuracy than BERT.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Holding parameters fixed and increasing pretraining data from 16 GB to 160 GB improves downstream accuracy, a direct demonstration of data scaling.

terminology.meaning: Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach: BERT-style encoder trained longer on more data with tweaked pretraining choices.

connections: p.480: loading RoBERTa with KerasHub (`roberta_base_en`), trained about a day on 1,024 GPUs
p.481: the backbone summary (124M parameters, 12 encoder layers)

paragraphs.excerpt: To use a pretrained model we will need a few things:
paragraphs.what_it_says: This line introduces a list of what is needed to use a pretrained model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The full list continues on p.480: a matching tokenizer, a matching model architecture, and the pretrained weights. All three must agree with how the model was pretrained.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A pretrained checkpoint is only useful together with the exact preprocessing and code that produced it; mismatches fail silently, giving garbage rather than errors.

paragraphs.excerpt: A matching tokenizer—Used with the pretrained model itself. Any text must be tokenized
paragraphs.what_it_says: The first requirement is a matching tokenizer: text must be tokenized as during pretraining. If IMDb words map to different indices than in pretraining, the model's learned token representations cannot be used (the sentence finishes on p.480).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The embedding matrix is indexed by token id. Row 133 of RoBERTa's embedding table was learned for whatever string RoBERTa's tokenizer maps to 133 ("The", per p.480). If your tokenizer maps a different word to 133, the model receives the wrong meaning for every token, and all pretrained knowledge is scrambled.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is why KerasHub ships the tokenizer and the backbone under the same preset name (`roberta_base_en`, p.480), and why the IMDb reviews in this section are re-tokenized with RoBERTa's tokenizer instead of the chapter 14 vectorizer (pp.482-483).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Token ids are just indices into the embedding table $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}$. A consistent vocabulary, splitting rules and special tokens (`<s>`, `</s>`, `<pad>`) are all part of the contract.

terminology.meaning: The mapping from raw text to a sequence of integer token ids, including the vocabulary and splitting rules.

connections: p.483: packing token ids with `<s>`, `</s>` and `<pad>` as in pretraining

concepts.name: Masked language modeling
concepts.definition: A self-supervised pretraining objective: randomly replace about 15% of tokens with `[MASK]` and train the model to predict the original tokens from the rest of the sequence.
concepts.intuition: A cloze test: fill in the blanks in a paragraph using clues from both sides.
concepts.technical: Loss is cross-entropy over the vocabulary, computed only at masked positions; the encoder sees the full corrupted sequence with bidirectional attention.
concepts.significance: Enables pretraining a bidirectional encoder on unlimited unlabeled text.
concepts.example: Input: "the [MASK] sat on the mat" → target at position 1: "cat".
concepts.misconception: That MLM predicts every token. Only the ~15% masked positions are scored, so each sequence gives fewer learning signals than causal LM does.

concepts.name: Causal language model
concepts.definition: A model of the probability of each token given the preceding tokens, $p(\text{token} \mid \text{past tokens})$.
concepts.intuition: Reading left to right and guessing the next word.
concepts.technical: Implemented with causal masking in a Transformer decoder or with an RNN; supports generation by sampling.
concepts.significance: Contrasted on this page with MLM; it is the basis of GPT-style generative models (chapter 16).
concepts.example: Given "the cat sat on the", predict "mat".
concepts.misconception: That the word 'causal' implies cause and effect. It just means each prediction depends only on earlier positions.

concepts.name: Contextual word embedding
concepts.definition: A token representation that depends on the surrounding words, produced by running the whole sequence through a pretrained Transformer.
concepts.intuition: A word's meaning shifts with its neighbors; the vector shifts too.
concepts.technical: Output of the final encoder layer at the token's position, shape (768,) per token for RoBERTa base (p.484).
concepts.significance: Much richer than the static embeddings of chapter 14; it is what makes BERT-style transfer powerful.
concepts.example: "bank" in "river bank" vs. "bank account" gets two different vectors.
concepts.misconception: That a pretrained Transformer is just a bigger lookup table of word vectors.

concepts.name: BERT / RoBERTa
concepts.definition: Pretrained Transformer encoders. BERT (Devlin et al. 2018) introduced MLM pretraining; RoBERTa (Liu et al. 2019) trained a slightly simplified variant on 10x more data.
concepts.intuition: Same engine, more fuel: RoBERTa is better mainly because it read ten times more text.
concepts.technical: Encoder-only, bidirectional self-attention; base size has 12 layers and a 768-dimensional hidden state (pp.481, 484).
concepts.significance: RoBERTa base is the backbone fine-tuned on IMDb in this section.
concepts.example: BERT pretraining: 16 GB of text; RoBERTa: 160 GB.
concepts.misconception: That RoBERTa's gains come mostly from architectural innovation. The book stresses the extra data.

concepts.name: Tokenizer-model matching
concepts.definition: The requirement that inputs to a pretrained model be tokenized exactly as during pretraining.
concepts.intuition: A codebook: send messages in a different code and the receiver reads nonsense.
concepts.technical: Token id $k$ selects row $k$ of the learned embedding matrix; any change in vocabulary or splitting breaks the correspondence.
concepts.significance: The first of three requirements for reusing a pretrained model (the others are on p.480).
concepts.example: RoBERTa maps "The" to id 133 (p.480); a chapter 14 vectorizer would assign it some other id.
concepts.misconception: That any reasonable tokenizer will do as long as the vocabulary size matches.

math.title: Causal vs. masked language modeling objectives
math.latex: \begin{aligned} \text{causal LM:}\quad & p(x_t \mid x_1, \dots, x_{t-1}) \\ \text{masked LM:}\quad & p(x_i \mid x_{\setminus M}),\; i \in M \end{aligned}

variables.meaning: the set of masked positions (about 15% of the sequence)
the surrounding, unmasked tokens on both sides

math.operations: Both are conditional distributions over the vocabulary computed by a softmax; they differ in what they condition on.
math.purpose: Formalizes the book's contrast between the two pretraining setups.
math.interpretation: The causal model can be sampled left to right to generate text; the masked model sees two-sided context, which gives better representations but no direct generation procedure.
math.intuition: Guessing the next word in a story vs. filling a blank in the middle of a sentence.
math.numerical_example: Sentence (8 tokens): "the movie was not good at all ." A causal LM is trained on 7 next-token predictions. An MLM masking 15% would hide about 1 token, e.g. "the movie was [MASK] good at all .", and predict "not" from both sides.

math.title: Masked language modeling loss
math.source_text: replace about 15% of the tokens with a special [MASK] token. The model will attempt to predict the original masked token values

variables.meaning: the corrupted input sequence, with masked positions replaced by `[MASK]`
the original token at masked position i (the target)

math.operations: Sum of cross-entropies over the masked positions only.
math.purpose: Makes precise what 'predict the original masked token values' means as a training loss.
math.interpretation: Lower loss means the model reconstructs hidden words better from context, which forces it to encode syntax and meaning.
math.intuition: Points are scored only on the blanks.
math.numerical_example: With $n = 512$, about $0.15 \times 512 \approx 77$ positions are masked per sequence. If the model assigns probability 0.5 to each correct token, the loss is $77 \times (-\ln 0.5) \approx 77 \times 0.693 \approx 53.4$ (or $0.693$ averaged per masked token).

deeper.title: Why bidirectional models can't simply generate
deeper.body: To generate, you need $p(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})$ for the next position. BERT was trained only on $p(x_i \mid \text{both sides})$ with some tokens masked; it never learned to predict with an empty right side. You could append `[MASK]` and ask for a fill, but the predictions are poorly calibrated for that use, and each new token changes every other token's representation (no caching). That is why the book says BERT is "not a model meant to run generation in a loop" and why chapter 16 builds a causal GPT-style model for generation.

deeper.title: Static vs. contextual embeddings, concretely
deeper.body: In chapter 14 a pretrained embedding is a table $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$: "bank" → $E[\text{bank}]$, always the same vector. In RoBERTa, the token embedding is only layer 0. Twelve encoder layers (p.481) then mix in information from other positions through attention. The final 768-dimensional vector for "bank" in "I sat on the river bank" therefore differs from the one in "I opened a bank account". Fine-tuning a classifier on such vectors lets it rely on disambiguated meanings, for example sarcasm or negation in movie reviews.

deeper.title: Back-of-the-envelope: how much text is 160 GB?
deeper.body: At roughly 1 byte per character and about 5-6 characters per English word (including space), 16 GB is on the order of 3 billion words and 160 GB about 30 billion words. The 10x increase is the main thing RoBERTa changed, and the book credits it for the noticeably better performance at equal parameter count. (Rough estimates, not from the book.)

misconceptions.claim: BERT is a different architecture from the Transformer encoder built in this chapter.
misconceptions.correction: The book says the structure is exactly the same as the encoder part of the translation Transformer; it is larger and trained differently.

misconceptions.claim: Masked language modeling requires labeled data.
misconceptions.correction: It is unsupervised: masks are chosen at random and the original tokens are the targets.

misconceptions.claim: RoBERTa beats BERT mainly due to a new architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The book says it made only minor simplifications; the most notable change is 10x more training data (160 GB vs. 16 GB).

misconceptions.claim: Any tokenizer with the same vocabulary size works with a pretrained model.
misconceptions.correction: Token ids must map to exactly the same strings as during pretraining, or the learned embeddings are meaningless for your inputs.

misconceptions.claim: BERT can be used directly as a text generator like GPT.
misconceptions.correction: Its bidirectional training makes it good for representations, not for generation in a loop.

takeaways: BERT is exactly a Transformer encoder: bidirectional, good for representations, not for generating text in a loop.
Masked language modeling hides about 15% of tokens and predicts them from both sides: p(token | surrounding tokens), vs. a causal LM's p(token | past tokens).
MLM is unsupervised, so huge unlabeled corpora (mostly Wikipedia for BERT) can be used.
Pretrained Transformers give contextual embeddings, a major step beyond static word embeddings.
RoBERTa is a lightly simplified BERT trained on 10x more data (160 GB vs. 16 GB), and performs noticeably better.
Reusing a pretrained model requires a matching tokenizer (plus matching architecture and weights, p.480).

questions.question: Which conditional distribution does a masked language model learn?
questions.explanation: The book contrasts the causal LM's p(token|past tokens) with the MLM's p(token|surrounding tokens). p(label|tokens) is a supervised classifier. Next-sentence prediction was a separate BERT objective that the book does not discuss (and RoBERTa dropped).

questions.question: Roughly what fraction of tokens is replaced by [MASK] in BERT's pretraining, and what is the training target?
questions.answer: About 15%; the target is the original token at each masked position.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Why is masked language modeling called unsupervised, and why did that matter for BERT?
questions.answer: The targets are the original tokens, obtained by masking random positions of any text, so no human labels are needed. This allowed collecting the very large amount of text that a 100M-300M parameter model requires.
questions.explanation: The book links model size to data needs and MLM's label-free setup to data availability.

questions.question: What does the book identify as the most notable difference between RoBERTa and BERT?
options: It uses 10x more training text (160 GB vs. 16 GB)
questions.answer: It uses 10x more training text (160 GB vs. 16 GB)
questions.explanation: RoBERTa made only minor architectural simplifications; the book stresses the extra data and better performance at equal parameter count. It remains encoder-only, uses subword tokenization (p.480), and its base model is BERT-base sized.

questions.question: What does a pretrained Transformer give that pretrained word embeddings from chapter 14 do not?
questions.answer: A representation of each word computed in the context of the surrounding words, so the same word gets different vectors in different sentences.
questions.explanation: Static embeddings map each word to one fixed vector; a Transformer encoder mixes in context through attention.

questions.question: A 512-token sequence is used for MLM with 15% masking. About how many positions contribute to the loss, and how does that compare with a causal LM on the same sequence?
questions.answer: About 77 positions (0.15 × 512 ≈ 76.8). A causal LM gets a prediction target at about 511 positions, so roughly 6-7x more training signal per sequence.
questions.explanation: MLM scores only masked positions. This lower sample efficiency is one reason MLM models need lots of data.

questions.question: Why must you use the matching tokenizer with a pretrained model?
questions.answer: Because token ids index the learned embedding table. If words map to different ids than during pretraining, the model looks up the wrong learned representations.
questions.explanation: This is the first of the requirements listed at the bottom of the page and continued on p.480.

questions.question: Can you explain to a friend why BERT is good for classifying movie reviews but not for writing them?
questions.answer: BERT sees the whole review at once through bidirectional attention and was trained to fill in blanks, so it builds rich representations, which is ideal for classification. It never learned to predict the next word from only the past, so it is not suited to generating text token by token.
questions.explanation: Check that your answer mentions bidirectionality and the training objective.
